newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN says Croats allow more Moslems to return home.
newsitem.headline: UN says Croats allow more Moslems to return home.

text.p: Some 350 Moslem refugees are due to return to their pre-war homes in central Bosnia this week after Croat officials allowed back a first group which had been expelled by mobs two weeks ago, the U.N. refugee agency said on Monday.

A first group of 99 mostly male Moslem refugees travelled in two buses back to their homes in the village of Kruscica near the central town of Jajce on Saturday without incident, spokeswoman Maki Shinohara of the Geneva-based UNHCR said.

A second group of 97 Moslems would return home to Lendici village near Jajce on Monday, followed by 56 returnees to the nearby village of Bucici on Tuesday, another 113 to Divicani village on Wednesday and 90 to Gornja Donja on Thursday.
Several hundred Moslems were forced to flee their villages in the Jajce area by hostile Croat mobs earlier this month in an incident which drew international condemnation.
U.N. relief officials and Western mediators brokered an agreement this week between Croat and Moslem authorities which called for the refugees to return to Jajce this month.
"If it all goes well, we hope this (agreement) will be a model for returns to other villages," Shinohara said.

The return of hundreds of thousands of displaced people to areas of Bosnia where they were the ethnic minority is seen as crucial to the success of the 1995 peace treaty that grants Moslem, Croat and Serb refugees the right to return home.

Nationalist authorities have tended to permit only members of their own ethnic community to move back. Some 800,000 Bosnians remain internally displaced and another 700,000 refugees have fled abroad according to UNHCR.
Moslems and Croats fought a 10-month war for territory in 1993 and later formed a federation which covers half of Bosnia.
Major powers have offered generous reconstruction aid to municipal authorities who comply with the peace treaty's provisions on refugee returns.
Following international pressure, Croat authorities in central Bosnia have recently shifted their stance and begun allowing Moslems to move back to their homes.
But Bosnian Croat leaders in the western Herzegovina region which borders neighbouring Croatia have steadfastly refused to make good on promises to permit Moslems or Serbs to return.
